title: Four Questions to Agni, Then Sit Down as Hotā
synthesis:
Five verses, and the first of them is nothing but questions. Not rhetorical ones — the hymn genuinely does not know what to bring, and says so before it says anything else.

*Kā te upetiḥ manaso varāya bhuvad agne śaṃtamā* — what approach of the mind would be most benign, for the choosing? Then: *kā manīṣā* — what insight? Then: who has ever compassed your *dakṣa*, your effective power, by means of *yajña*s? And last: *kena vā te manasā dāśema* — with what mind, then, shall we give to you? Four questions in one verse, and two of them turn on the same word. The verse opens on *manasaḥ* and closes on *manasā*: what is being asked is not what to place in the fire but what state to be in while placing it. The second verse answers by changing the subject, and the answer is hidden in a word. Come here, {{agni}}, sit down as *hotā* — the one who offers and who calls the gods by name — *adabdhaḥ*, undeceived and undeceivable; be our *supuraetā*, our good forerunner. May the two world-halves, all-pervading, favour you. And then the purpose: *yaja mahe saumanasāya devān* — sacrifice to the gods for great *saumanasa*, good-mindedness. The worshipper asked with what *manas* he should give; the rite is performed so that *manas* may come out well. That is the whole hymn in miniature, and it is stated three words at a time across two verses.

The third verse turns outward. Burn up all the *rakṣas*es; become the *abhiśastipāvā* of the sacrifices — the one who cleanses them of curse and imprecation, the officer whose job is to keep the rite from being spoiled by hostile speech. And then bring here the lord of {{soma}} with his two tawny horses: *ātithyam asmai cakṛma sudāvne*, we have made the guest-welcome ready for the generous one. The guest is not named. He does not have to be; the two bays name him.

The fourth verse gives Agni the offices themselves. He is *vahni*, the conveyor, called with his mouth and with *prajāvatā vacasā*, speech that brings offspring. Sit here with the gods, the verse says, and then: *veṣi hotram uta potram* — you perform the *hotra* and the *potra*, the calling office and the cleansing office both. In a full rite these belong to two different men. Here one god holds both, which is the practical form of the claim that Agni is where the whole rite converges. He is addressed at the close as *prayantaḥ janitaḥ vasūnām*, the giver and begetter of goods, and asked simply to be awake.

The fifth verse finally answers the first. What approach works? The one that has worked. *Yathā viprasya manuṣo havirbhir devān ayajaḥ kavibhiḥ kaviḥ san* — as, with the oblations of the wise Manu, you sacrificed to the gods, a seer among seers, so today, O *hotar satyatara*, most true of callers, sacrifice with the gladdening ladle. The question of verse 1 was answered not by a rule but by a precedent. Nobody has to invent the right approach; it was found once, and the fire that carried it is the same fire.
practice:
This is the hymn for the moment before the rite, when the question is not what to do but how to be while doing it. A worshipper who has ever sat down before the lamp and wondered whether the mind he has brought is fit for it is standing exactly where verse 1 stands. The Ṛgveda's answer is not reassurance. It is that the mind is what the rite works on — *yaja mahe saumanasāya*, sacrifice for great good-mindedness. You do not need to arrive with the right *manas*; the offering is how it is acquired.

Two of the offices named here still structure a śrauta rite. The *hotā* calls and offers; the *potṛ* purifies. In the classical sixteen-priest arrangement these are separate men serving separate deities, and the hymn's claim that Agni does both is a claim about where authority in the rite actually sits. [[1.94]].6, by the same collection's arrangement only eighteen sūktas later, extends the same list further — *adhvaryu*, *hotā*, *praśāstā*, *potā*, *purohita* — and gives Agni all of them.

The third verse names a fear that has not gone away. *Abhiśasti* is hostile speech, the curse or the accusation, and Agni is asked to be the one who cleanses a rite of it. Anyone who has performed something carefully while knowing it was being spoken against has that verse.

This is the third of Gotama Rāhūgaṇa's sūktas, and the run he holds is unusual. The Anukramaṇī gives him 1.74 through 1.93 without a break — twenty consecutive sūktas, the second-longest unbroken stretch under one name in maṇḍala 1, behind Dīrghatamas at 1.140–1.164 — plus one more at 9.31. Reading 1.76 with [[1.77]] and [[1.78]] beside it is reading one man's sustained work on one god, not three unrelated hymns; the same Agni is addressed, the questions accumulate, and the family name closes them.
disagreements:
Verse 1's *kā manīṣā* divides the translators, and one of them appears to have slipped. The padapāṭha reads *kā manīṣā* — what insight, what considered thought — which Griffith renders "What hymn of praise shall bring us greatest blessing?" Wilson prints "what can a hundred encomiums (effect)", which corresponds to nothing in the word-division and looks like a misreading rather than a variant.

On verse 2, Sāyaṇa is concrete where the translators are general: *ni sīda*, sit down, means sit down in the chamber where the burnt offerings are presented — the hymn is telling Agni where in the enclosure to be, not merely inviting him.

Verse 3's guest is unnamed in the Sanskrit, and Sāyaṇa supplies the identification: *somapati*, lord of soma, is a remarkable epithet for {{indra}}, indicated not by the name but by *haribhyām*, the two bays, which belong to Indra alone. Wilson accordingly prints "( Indra )" in brackets; Griffith leaves "the Lord of Soma" unglossed and lets the reader make the inference the Sanskrit intends.

Verse 4's *bodhi* is read by Wilson as transitive — "awaken us" — and by Griffith the same way. The form is more naturally an imperative of √bhū or √budh addressed to Agni himself, which would make it "be aware", and the ambiguity is not resolved by the witnesses here.
